payload.rationale: No current data supplied, so this rests on background knowledge through early 2026. 2025 ended with roughly 2,000+ US measles cases (highest since 1992). 2026 opened at a much faster pace: a large Upstate South Carolina outbreak (hundreds of cases by January, approaching ~1,000 by mid-February), continuing Utah/Arizona transmission, and scattered importations, putting the national 2026 count plausibly above 1,000 within the first ~6-7 weeks. A simple annualization of that early pace would approach or exceed 6,000, but measles outbreaks in the US typically burn out as susceptible pools in affected communities are exhausted and vaccination campaigns take hold; the Texas 2025 outbreak followed this pattern, with the national count decelerating sharply after spring. A central expectation of roughly 2,500–4,500 cases for 2026 seems most plausible, with 6,000 requiring either sustained SC-scale transmission for many months or one or more additional large undervaccinated-community outbreaks in the second half of the year. Reasons the estimate could be too high: outbreaks likely peaked in Q1 and declined, and CDC counts (which exclude late revisions after expiration) may lag; the threshold is roughly triple the 2025 total. Reasons it could be too low: by the September 2026 forecast date the actual trajectory is largely known and unknown to me; loss of US elimination status and declining MMR coverage raise the chance of endemic-style spread, and the early-2026 pace was far above any recent year, so a 6,000+ year is a real possibility.
limitations: No supplied evidence; relies on memory of early-2026 case counts which may be imprecise.
Actual 2026 case data through September 2026 is unknown to the forecaster despite the forecast date.
Resolution depends on CDC's specific reporting and revision rules at expiration.
Outbreak dynamics are highly variable and depend on local vaccination coverage.
